chapter.learnerQuestion: What water actually reached the active root zone, how evenly was it distributed, and how quickly did the root environment move from wetting toward dryback?

sourceContext.citation: Oregon State University Extension. Optimum irrigation for CBD-type hemp plants in the field. EM 9571. July 2024.
sourceContext.supports: Hemp response to irrigation varies with cultivar type, plant density, irrigation method, climate and seasonal water demand, so irrigation should not be reduced to one universal volume.

sourceContext.citation: Penn State Extension. Drip Irrigation for Vegetable Production.
sourceContext.supports: Irrigation frequency and amount depend on crop water use, root-zone water storage, soil texture and wetting pattern; drip systems should be managed from the root-zone reservoir rather than runtime alone.

sourceContext.citation: University of Minnesota Extension. Evapotranspiration-based irrigation scheduling or water-balance method.
sourceContext.supports: Root-zone water status can be monitored directly with soil-moisture methods or estimated from a water balance that separates precipitation, irrigation, crop water use, runoff and deep percolation.

sourceContext.citation: Penn State Extension. Making Drip Irrigation Decisions After Rain in Plasticulture. 2026.
sourceContext.supports: Rainfall contribution to the root zone depends on surface cover, soil texture, lateral movement and crop rooting; rainfall totals alone do not prove equivalent root-zone recharge.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Measure rainfall as an input, then verify root-zone recharge
subtopics.goal: Separate rain depth from the amount and distribution of water that actually reaches active roots.

measure.method: Use an on-site rain gauge when possible and record the event start/end time. If using a nearby station, record station identity and distance so the value is clearly labeled off-site.

measure.metric: Root-zone moisture before and after rain
measure.unit: volumetric water content, sensor units, or defined qualitative class at fixed depth
measure.method: Measure the same marked points and depths before rain when possible, then after the event and during subsequent drainage/dryback. Keep sensor/method and depth consistent.
measure.frequency: Before representative events, after rain, and during dryback.

measure.method: Use a probe, soil core, or calibrated moisture profile to identify how deeply the event changed moisture. Avoid aggressive excavation near important roots.
measure.frequency: After representative light, moderate and heavy rain events.

measure.unit: duration + mapped location or ordinal class
measure.method: Record visible runoff paths, ponding time, mulch/plastic shedding, channeling, or dry sheltered zones that explain why rain depth and root-zone response differ.
measure.frequency: During or immediately after representative events.

record: rain gauge/station source and event duration
photos of representative wetting or runoff patterns
compare: rain depth against measured change in root-zone moisture
different depths and positions within the same planting area
similar rainfall events under different antecedent moisture or surface-cover conditions
interpret: The same rainfall depth can produce different root-zone recharge because infiltration, interception, runoff, surface cover and prior moisture differ.
Rain can wet the surface while deeper active roots remain comparatively dry, or saturate low zones while raised/container zones drain rapidly.
A rain event should therefore modify irrigation decisions only after its root-zone effect is verified or reasonably estimated.
subtopics.decisionRule: Do not cancel or schedule irrigation from rainfall total alone. Verify moisture at relevant depths/positions and adjust only after identifying how much of the root zone actually changed.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: On-site depth-specific moisture measurements provide stronger evidence than a regional rainfall total. Qualitative hand-feel observations should remain labeled qualitative.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Verify that irrigation wets the intended root volume
subtopics.goal: Measure delivery and wetting geometry so runtime is connected to actual root-zone coverage.

measure.method: Collect from representative emitters/outlets for a timed interval in a known-volume container. Test near, middle and far positions when pressure loss or clogging is possible.
measure.frequency: At setup, after maintenance, and whenever uneven delivery is suspected.

measure.unit: L or gallons per irrigation event
measure.method: Calculate measured flow multiplied by runtime for each emitter/zone or use a calibrated flow meter. Record whether the value is measured or calculated.
measure.frequency: For representative irrigation events and after system changes.

measure.unit: cm or inches from emitter and below surface
measure.method: After irrigation, probe or measure moisture at fixed distances and depths from the emitter. Use a repeatable grid so the wetting shape can be compared as roots expand.
measure.frequency: At establishment, mid-season, and after emitter/layout/runtime changes.

measure.unit: individual emitter volumes and optional % uniformity
measure.method: Collect the same-duration output from multiple representative emitters. Compare the lowest-output locations with the overall sample rather than relying on one convenient emitter.
measure.frequency: At setup and periodically during the season.

compare: near, middle and far delivery points
wetting pattern early season vs later root expansion
measured delivered volume against observed root-zone moisture response
interpret: A consistent runtime does not guarantee a consistent delivered volume when pressure, clogging, line length or source flow changes.
As roots expand, an early-season wetting bulb can become too narrow even if the same irrigation volume still prevents immediate wilt.
Soil texture affects wetting geometry; sandy and fine-textured soils can distribute drip water differently.
subtopics.decisionRule: Change emitter placement, number, runtime or system maintenance when the measured wetting pattern no longer covers the intended active root volume or when sampled outputs become meaningfully uneven.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: Wetting radius/depth observed at one event is condition-specific. Recheck after major root growth, soil drying, emitter changes or seasonal demand shifts.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Measure how mulch changes dryback and root-zone temperature
subtopics.goal: Quantify the effect of surface cover on evaporation, temperature and moisture distribution instead of assuming mulch always changes irrigation in the same way.

measure.method: Measure at the same depth under mulch and at a defined comparison point. Record time of day, surface condition and weather.
measure.frequency: During representative hot/cool periods and after mulch changes.

measure.metric: Moisture under mulch vs comparison point
measure.unit: matched sensor units or qualitative class at fixed depth
measure.method: Use the same measurement method and depth under the mulched zone and at an unmulched/reference zone when a valid comparison is available.
measure.frequency: Before irrigation/rain and through representative dryback intervals.

measure.unit: hours or days between defined moisture states
measure.method: Choose a repeatable starting and comparison state using the same sensor or qualitative class, then record elapsed time under comparable weather.
Inspect the mulch/soil interface immediately around the stem base separately from the wider root zone and record persistent contact with wet material.
measure.frequency: After irrigation/rain and during routine scouting.

compare: mulched and reference zones at the same time/depth
dryback before and after adding or changing mulch
stem-base conditions against the wider root-zone condition
interpret: Mulch can reduce evaporative loss and buffer temperature, but its effect depends on material, coverage, weather and irrigation placement.
A moist surface under mulch does not prove the deeper root zone is adequately wet, and a dry exposed surface does not prove deeper roots are dry.
Keeping the stem base as a separate observation prevents the broader benefits of mulch from hiding a localized persistently wet interface.
subtopics.decisionRule: Adjust irrigation only after comparing the new dryback/root-zone pattern created by mulch. Keep a distinct stem-base inspection point rather than treating all covered soil as one condition.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: Mulch effects are site-specific. Use repeated matched measurements instead of importing evaporation or temperature reductions from a different material or climate.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Track drainage, salts and root condition as one root-zone system
subtopics.goal: Detect when repeated irrigation or restricted drainage creates persistent saturation, salt accumulation or root stress that foliage alone cannot identify.

measure.unit: minutes or hours to a defined moisture state
measure.method: After a known irrigation/rain event, measure the same depth/point until it leaves the defined saturated/wet state. Record the criterion used.
measure.frequency: During representative high-volume events and when root stress is suspected.

measure.method: Measure a representative source-water sample with a calibrated EC meter and record temperature compensation/meter details when available.
measure.frequency: Baseline and whenever the source or season changes.

measure.metric: Root-zone / extract / leachate EC when method is appropriate
measure.unit: mS/cm or µS/cm with method named
measure.method: Use a documented soil/media extraction or leachate method appropriate to the production system. Do not compare numbers from different extraction methods as if they are identical.
measure.frequency: Baseline for managed media/containers and when salt accumulation is suspected.

measure.method: Where roots can be observed without damaging the crop, record color, odor, firmness, visible lesions and distribution. Pair observations with moisture/drainage history.
measure.frequency: During transplant, troubleshooting, or planned root inspections.

record: source-water EC and meter calibration status
root-zone EC method and value when measured
compare: source-water EC against root-zone trend using a consistent method
root observations before and after correcting water/drainage problems
interpret: Persistent saturation can reduce root-zone aeration even when leaves are being interpreted as a nutrient problem.
EC is method-dependent and reflects dissolved ions, not the identity or plant availability of each nutrient.
Outdoor rainfall can leach salts in some systems, but covered containers, protected root zones, repeated fertigation or limited drainage can still accumulate salts.
subtopics.decisionRule: When stress coincides with slow drainage or rising EC, investigate water movement and root condition before increasing fertilizer. Correct the root-zone process that is generating the pattern rather than treating leaf color alone.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: EC values are only comparable when units, sample method, dilution/extraction and meter calibration are known. Root appearance alone does not identify a specific pathogen or nutrient disorder.

fieldWorksheet.title: Section 3 water & root-zone field record
fields: rain depth or delivered irrigation volume
root-zone/leachate EC method + value when used
decision and what evidence would change it
fieldWorksheet.outcome: The learner should finish with a water record that distinguishes input volume from root-zone recharge, verifies distribution, tracks dryback and identifies drainage or salinity concerns with explicit measurement context.

calculationHelpers.name: Delivered irrigation volume
calculationHelpers.use: Translate emitter/system flow and runtime into an estimated delivered volume.
calculationHelpers.boundary: The calculation does not prove uniform delivery or root-zone capture.

calculationHelpers.name: Sample delivery uniformity
calculationHelpers.formula: low-quarter average collected volume ÷ overall average collected volume × 100
calculationHelpers.use: Screen a set of sampled emitters for uneven delivery.
calculationHelpers.boundary: A small sample is a screening tool, not a full irrigation-system audit; sampling design matters.

calculationHelpers.name: Root-zone water-balance estimate
calculationHelpers.formula: current deficit ≈ previous deficit + crop water use − precipitation − irrigation
calculationHelpers.use: Provide a weather-based planning estimate when crop-water-use data and an initial root-zone condition are available.
calculationHelpers.boundary: Runoff, deep percolation, interception and inaccurate crop coefficients can make the estimate diverge from measured soil water; direct root-zone checks remain important.

calculationHelpers.name: Dryback interval
calculationHelpers.formula: time at comparison moisture state − time after defined wetting state
calculationHelpers.use: Compare how quickly the same root zone dries under different weather, mulch or plant-size conditions.
calculationHelpers.boundary: Only compare intervals that use the same moisture definition, depth and measurement method.
